0.6.5.en: A Light Remote with a “Set colour” button added to it would finish setting up and then be unavailable straight away, saying only that its configuration could not be read. It was readable all along — the check that reads it back on every start had never been told about that one job. Any remote sitting unavailable for this reason comes back with all of its buttons exactly as you set them up, with nothing to redo. Separately, “Or press a button to find it” has been removed from the remote list, along with the screen it opened and the indicator on the buttons screen that followed a real press. It was never reliable enough to be the way you would do it, and some remotes cannot be heard at all, so the list was always the path that works. Picking a remote from the list is unchanged. Lightkeeper's devices now show what they want your lights to be — a brightness, a colour temperature, the colour, how light it is outside — so you can use those values in your own Flows as tags, and see them in Insights. A new card sets a room from two Lightkeeper devices at once, taking the colour from one and the brightness from another in a single change rather than three visible steps, and it only switches lights on if you ask it to. A new condition asks a Room-sensing Light whether it is dark enough, using the thresholds you already set up. Lights set up to follow a colour through the day now come on already the right colour, instead of coming on as they were and changing a second or two later. Setting the colour before the lights come on has been possible since 0.4, but no setup screen ever showed the switch for it, so nobody could turn it on. Both screens now have it, along with a button that tries it on one of your own lights and tells you what happened. It is on for newly added devices; devices you already have are left exactly as you set them up. If a light ever does come on by itself from it, Lightkeeper turns it off for that device and does not try again. Brightness is still never set in advance, because that would switch the light on. Separately, a light that accepts an instruction and then ignores it is no longer mistaken for somebody changing it by hand: that mistake made Lightkeeper leave the light alone for four hours, and on some lights it could repeat indefinitely, so a room could sit unattended all evening while everything reported itself as working. Eleven fixes from a general review of the whole app, none of which anything already running could see. The two worth knowing about. A Colour Curve Light set to follow sunrise or sunset at one of its points would quietly stop changing anything at all — and it would also leave the Lightkeeper settings page blank, so the one screen you would open to find out why showed you nothing. That kind of point is refused now, and a device that cannot describe itself is left off the page instead of taking the page down with it. And in the Flows section, the button that deletes leftover Flows asks you to approve a specific list first; a request that skipped that step used to go ahead and delete anyway. It refuses now, and it also refuses when Lightkeeper cannot read its own devices, rather than treating the ones it could not see as gone. The rest: trying a circadian light's colours out and then closing the screen without pressing "Put them back" meant that the NEXT light you set up restored the wrong lamps when you pressed it there; a sensor's week grid named the wrong days for any week containing a clock change; a Light Remote named with nothing but spaces ended up with no name at all; an API key that Homey rejects left a connection open every time you tried one, and trying a bad key no longer interrupts the check running against the key you already had; a paused schedule quietly re-checked every one of its Flows twice a day forever; deleting a Light Remote or a schedule left a small record behind that nothing ever removed; and one unusual Flow card from another app could stop Lightkeeper finding any remote at all. Four more problems were closed before they could happen to anyone, and some stale duplicated text that had been shipping inside two of the setup screens is gone. A day of real diagnostics from a household running six of these devices showed six more things. A Room-sensing Light whose sensor sits in the room it lights can push itself brighter and brighter; Lightkeeper watched for that and only spoke up after seeing it five times, having seen it about twice a day and forgotten the count on every restart and every edit. It now remembers, and the settings page shows what it has seen so far. A light that declines a colour while it is switched off used to be re-tried every time it came on, which in a room on a motion sensor meant hundreds of refused writes a day; after three such switch-ons it is left alone and tried again the next day. A light sensor that stops reporting altogether now says so on the device, after half a day of silence — that warning used to exist only during setup. And three diagnostics improvements: the failure list is no longer filled by the one expected failure, a device no longer reports a brightness it stopped following, and memory is now reported over time rather than as a single number. Lights that fade slowly to a new setting are no longer mistaken for somebody taking them over by hand, so a room whose lamps take their time stays on its schedule instead of being left alone for hours. A remote button can now do a tenth thing: turn the lights on the way the rest of your house already knows they should look. Pick which of your other Lightkeeper devices it takes the colour and warmth from, and which one it takes the brightness from, and it reads both at the moment you press — so a button set up in February is still right in June. Each choice shows what that setup is producing right now, so three curves are told apart by what they are doing rather than by what you called them. A switch on the same card makes a second press turn the lights off again, which makes one button a whole light switch. Everything lands in one change rather than three visible steps, and if the setup a button follows is ever deleted the button still turns the lights on — it just cannot say what colour. Switching a light on or off is no longer mistaken for somebody taking it over by hand. A light that comes back on reports the level it was last showing, a few seconds after it comes on, and that used to read as a person moving it — in one room it meant the lights were left unattended for the whole twenty-nine minutes they were on. A light that fades out as it switches off reports itself part-way down about half a minute before it reports itself off, which read the same way. Both are understood now, and switching a light on and then dimming it yourself is still recognised as you. Lightkeeper's own record of what it has been doing also no longer fills up with routine entries about its own changes, so a bug report now reaches back days rather than hours. The setup screens have been redrawn to match the design across all five device types — colours, spacing and wording. A schedule block is now given a colour from the same set a Colour Curve Light uses, instead of a warmth slider; lamps that cannot do colour get the matching warmth, so a block does the same thing to every light in the room. Two blocks that overlap can be merged into one from the screen that warns about them. A schedule’s last screen now shows the day it just described, with its blocks on it. When you have no light sensor, the brightness screen now shows where the sun is today and what the lamps will do as it arrives. Opening Lightkeeper on a Homey with no lights is now a screen that offers a way out rather than one grey line. And an API key that Homey accepts but will not build Flows with now stays on screen, masked, with the one thing that saves the next attempt: permissions cannot be added to a key after it is made. The switch for setting the colour before lights come on is not drawn for the moment while where it belongs is settled — nothing about how your lights behave changes, and devices keep the setting they already have.

0.6.0.en: A fifth kind of device. A Room-sensing Light sets your lights' brightness from how much light is in the room already, dimming them as the morning comes up and lifting them again as it goes — or the other way round if you would rather the room followed the day. It works out how light it is from a light sensor you already own, and most motion sensors have one, or from how high the sun is using your Homey's own location. It needs no API key, only dims lights that are already on, and never switches one on or off. Every setup screen has also been redrawn: one question at a time, and a review of everything before it saves. Circadian lights now describe three parts of the day, with the boundaries following your own sunrise and sunset through the year instead of a fixed clock. On a Light Remote, each button can drive its own lights. Also fixed: a light that quietly returns to its own settings after Lightkeeper changes it is no longer mistaken for you taking over by hand, which could leave that light alone for days. Finally, three device types are renamed: Light controller to Light Remote, Curve light to Colour Curve Light, and Daylight light to Room-sensing Light. Only the names change — devices you have already added keep working, keep the name you gave them, and keep their settings and Flows.

0.5.2.en: Four fixes, all on the light-following device types. A Curve light could keep the colour it last held instead of going back to white: a curve that mixes coloured points with plain warmth points switched correctly the first time and then stopped switching back, because the lamp was never told to leave colour mode. The dimmest brightness setting no longer means off, either. Five per cent worked out to nothing at the lamp once converted, so lights set that low went dark rather than dim; the lowest setting is now ten per cent, and any curve point, schedule or circadian light already set below that has been moved up to it. Blends between two colours far apart on the wheel, amber to ocean say, now fade through pale instead of swinging round through purple and magenta on the way; colours close together look the same as they always did. And a bug report now says which of a curve's points carry a colour and what colour each light was last sent, none of which it could tell you before.

0.5.1.en: A tidier App Store listing. The description is much shorter and gets to the point, this What's new section reads as a paragraph instead of a wall of markup, and the four device icons have been redrawn so they are legible in the small circle the store draws them in. Nothing about how the app works has changed.

0.5.0.en: New: a Curve light, which is the circadian light with the whole day open to you. Set what your lights should look like at every point you choose, and give any of those points a colour instead of a warmth, from candle and amber through to ocean and forest. Lights that cannot show a colour follow the warmth instead, so the day looks the same shape on every lamp. The circadian light is simpler now: it asks two questions, what your lights should look like at their warmest and at their coolest, and handles the rest of the day itself. An existing circadian light keeps those two points and drops the ones in between; nothing stops working and nothing needs setting up again, and a curve you want back is a Curve light away. Also fixed: two schedules whose times overlap on the same lights no longer fight, a schedule refuses to run rather than guess the day when it cannot read your Homey's timezone, a remote whose buttons and dial share one Flow card now gets one Flow per button and direction, every screen stays light even when your phone is set to dark mode, and Lightkeeper uses less memory on your Homey.

0.4.0.en: New: a circadian light. Pick your lights, set how warm they should be through the day, and they follow it: the right colour the moment they come on, and adjusted while they stay on. It never switches lights on or off, and it needs no API key. Optionally follows brightness too, and can set the colour before the lights come on. Change a light by hand and it leaves that light alone until you switch it off and on again.

0.3.1.en: Generated Flows are now grouped in a folder per device, inside the Lightkeeper folder, so it is obvious which Flows came from which controller or schedule. Rename a device and its folder follows; delete it and the folder goes too. Flows made before this update move themselves the next time the device checks in, except any you had moved into a folder of your own, which stay exactly where you put them. The device type for remotes is now called Light controller instead of Remote-to-light controller, and nothing else changes: your existing devices, mappings and Flows are untouched.

0.3.0.en: New look. The app has a new icon, new colours taken from it, and new pictures for both device types, including a proper timer for the schedule device. Every screen in the app now uses the new colours. Fixed: a pairing or repair screen no longer waits forever when Homey does not answer, so you can try again instead of watching a screen that never finishes, and when a remote turns out to offer no usable events, a bug report now lists the trigger cards that were considered and why each was turned down.

0.2.2.en: New artwork throughout. The app icon is a lighthouse now, which suits the name better than the old remote-and-bulb, and the two device icons are drawn to match it. The app's picture in the store shows lamps lit in an evening room instead of a hand holding a remote, because the app does more than remotes, and the schedule device now has a picture of a lamp rather than a drawing of a clock face.

0.2.1.en: Fixed: warm and cold were the wrong way round. A schedule set to the warmest setting lit the room cold white, and on a remote the warmer button made the light colder. Both now go the way they say. If you set a warmth on a schedule before this update, open it and check the setting still reads the way you want it.

0.2.0.en: New: light schedules. Add a schedule device, pick your lights, and say when they come on and when they go off, after a while or at a set time. Up to twelve schedules per device, on the days you choose, optionally at a brightness and warmth you set. Each schedule device has its own switch, so you can pause the whole thing while you are away without losing any of it. The app is now called Lightkeeper, because it does more than link a remote to a light. Editing a generated Flow by hand is also noticed in more cases now, including changing the time on one: Lightkeeper leaves your edit alone and asks you to repair instead of quietly overwriting it.

0.1.0.en: First release. Point a paired remote, switch, button or rotary dial at your lights, and control on/off, brightness and colour temperature across individual lights or whole zones. Lightkeeper creates and maintains the Flows behind each mapping for you. Connects locally, for Homey Pro 2023 and later.

0.1.1.en: Fixed: repair now opens. It failed with an internal file error before any screen appeared, so a controller that needed repair had no way to be fixed. Giving a button a job another button already had now says so next to both controls; the notice used to sit at the bottom of the screen, below every light, where nobody saw it, and the control that lost its job quietly went back to Not assigned. App settings now show the API key status in colour: green when a working key is saved, amber when none is saved yet, red when a saved key has stopped working.
